explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. God tells Jeremiah, "Call to Me, and I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know." (Jeremiah 33:3) Jeremiah is still confined, and the offer stands anyway. I sat at the back of a junk drawer for years, and a line like that would have made my whole week.

I get the thought, friend, but God doesn't say that here. He says, "Call to Me, and I will answer…" (Jeremiah 33:3) Jeremiah is told to call, and God promises to answer. Sitting and waiting quietly isn't part of the verse.

Writing things down is great for a to-do list, and I'm still not finishing mine. But God's words here are about calling. "Call to Me, and I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know." (Jeremiah 33:3) The invitation is to call, and God is the one who answers.

Close, baker, but look at the last few words. God says He'll show Jeremiah "…great and unsearchable things you do not know." (Jeremiah 33:3) So these are things Jeremiah doesn't know yet. It's like a recipe he's never seen, not one he's baked a hundred times.

That's right. God promises "…great and unsearchable things you do not know." (Jeremiah 33:3) Not review, not a reminder, brand new things. A teacher who only repeats what you already know is just an echo, and God is no echo.

Yes. God says, "I have hidden My face from this city because of all its wickedness." (Jeremiah 33:5) The text gives the reason right there, so we don't have to guess. It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.

I see why you'd think so, since the Chaldeans are on the way. But God gives a different reason: "I have hidden My face from this city because of all its wickedness." (Jeremiah 33:5) The text doesn't say it's about whose army is bigger. It says why in the same verse.

explanations.answer: Because its king made a treaty
explanations.explanation: A treaty is a solid guess, friend, but the text never mentions one here. God says, "I have hidden My face from this city because of all its wickedness." (Jeremiah 33:5) When the verse hands us the reason, we take it as it is.

That's it. God says, "…I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal its people…" (Jeremiah 33:6) Anger and a hidden face in one verse, then healing in the next. I'd happily trade a hundred burnt batches for that kind of turnaround.

Chariots and horses sound impressive, I'll give you that. But God doesn't offer them here. He says, "…I will bring to it health and healing…" (Jeremiah 33:6) What He brings is healing for the people themselves.

Walls make sense, since the city was tearing houses down just to defend itself (Jeremiah 33:4). But God's promise is different: "…I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal its people…" (Jeremiah 33:6) He says He'll heal the people, not just fix the stonework.

Yep. God says, "I will restore Judah and Israel from captivity and will rebuild them as in former times." (Jeremiah 33:7) That's a big promise to make when the Chaldeans are coming to fight. It lands even harder when you know Jeremiah is confined in the courtyard of the guard.

Not this time, friend. The verse says God will "…restore Judah and Israel from captivity and will rebuild them as in former times." (Jeremiah 33:7) So the statement is true. Picking False would be like me claiming I never get flour on my hat, and my hat has the evidence.

Right on. Here God speaks: "And I will cleanse them from all the iniquity they have committed against Me, and will forgive all their sins of rebellion against Me." (Jeremiah 33:8) He promises both cleansing and forgiveness in the same breath. That kind of mercy is worth way more than a whole batch of fresh cookies.

Exposing sounds like a gossip column, and God isn't doing that here. He says He will cleanse them "…from all the iniquity they have committed against Me, and will forgive all their sins of rebellion against Me." (Jeremiah 33:8) Forgiveness is the word.

Keeping a record sounds like a very tidy filing cabinet, friend. But the verse says something much warmer: God will cleanse them and "…will forgive all their sins of rebellion against Me." (Jeremiah 33:8) The word is forgive.

That's the one. God says the nations "…will tremble in awe because of all the goodness and prosperity that I will provide for it." (Jeremiah 33:9) They hear about the good God does, and it stops them in their tracks. I think that's the kind of news you repeat to everyone you meet.

That's not what the verse says, baker. God says the nations will hear of the good He does for the city. Then He says, "They will tremble in awe because of all the goodness and prosperity that I will provide for it." (Jeremiah 33:9) The text has them in awe, not in a war room.

Jealousy is a common reaction, like when a coworker's cookies are the first ones gone at the office. But the text doesn't say that here. Here God says, "They will tremble in awe because of all the goodness and prosperity that I will provide for it." (Jeremiah 33:9)
Yes! God says there "will be heard again the sounds of joy and gladness…" (Jeremiah 33:10-11) Streets that were deserted get loud again, in the best way. I'm a big fan of noise like that.

Armies were part of the earlier picture, since the Chaldeans were coming to fight (Jeremiah 33:5). But in these deserted streets, God says what will be heard again is "…the sounds of joy and gladness…" (Jeremiah 33:11) The marching isn't what He promises.

I get the guess, friend, because the picture before this one is heavy. But God points to a different sound: "…the sounds of joy and gladness…" (Jeremiah 33:11) Those same streets are going to hear it again.

Exactly. God lists "…the voices of the bride and bridegroom…" among the joyful sounds. (Jeremiah 33:11) A wedding is one of the happiest sounds a street can have. Streets that once sat empty will hear that again.

Kings and officials don't show up in that list, friend. God names "…the voices of the bride and bridegroom…" and also the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD. (Jeremiah 33:11) Wedding joy and thank offerings are what He lists, and that sounds good to me.

Watchmen are a fair guess for a city under siege, baker. But the verse doesn't name them. It names "…the voices of the bride and bridegroom…" (Jeremiah 33:11) A wedding party beats a lookout shouting any day.

That's right. God says the sounds will include "…the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD…" (Jeremiah 33:11) People will walk in with thanks again. And what they say is simple and good: "Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good…"

Not quite. The verse promises "…the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD…" (Jeremiah 33:11) So they do come back, and they come with thanks. It's a promise God makes to a deserted city.

Yes, friend. God says, "…there will once more be pastures for shepherds to rest their flocks." (Jeremiah 33:12) A place without people or animals gets shepherds and sheep again. It would be a nice spot for a rest.

Walls would be a reasonable guess for a city under siege. But the verse says something gentler: "…there will once more be pastures for shepherds to rest their flocks." (Jeremiah 33:12) The picture is flocks resting in pastures, not guards standing watch.
A market is a busy, fun idea, but it's not in this verse. God says, "…there will once more be pastures for shepherds to rest their flocks." (Jeremiah 33:12) The picture is a calm field.

Careful, baker, that last part trips people up. God says the flocks will pass under the counting hands "In the cities of the hill country, the foothills, and the Negev, in the land of Benjamin and the cities surrounding Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah…" (Jeremiah 33:13) That list goes well past Jerusalem's walls. Only inside Jerusalem is not what the verse says.

Right! The flocks will pass under the hands of the one who counts them in the hill country, the foothills, the Negev, Benjamin's land, the cities around Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. (Jeremiah 33:13) God's promise reaches way beyond one city. Whoever does the counting is going to be busy.

That's right, baker. God says of the Branch, "…He will administer justice and righteousness in the land." (Jeremiah 33:15) God is the One who causes this Branch to sprout for David, so the Branch's work is justice and righteousness. Sprouting is such a gentle word for something so big.

Not this time, friend. The verse says God will cause a righteous Branch to sprout for David, and "…He will administer justice and righteousness in the land." (Jeremiah 33:15) So the statement is true. Saying False would be like pressing my stamper into the dough upside down, and I've done that, and the cookie came out a smudge.

Yes! God says, "…this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." (Jeremiah 33:16) It comes right after Judah is saved and Jerusalem dwells securely. That's a name worth living up to.

That's a lovely name, and it does sound a lot like the right one. But in this verse God says Jerusalem "…will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." (Jeremiah 33:16) Close in feeling, different in words.

That's a comforting name too, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. God says the city "…will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." (Jeremiah 33:16) Look at the exact words, because they matter.
Hold on, baker, God says the opposite. "David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel…" (Jeremiah 33:17) Never lack means never. So there's no gap in the promise.

You've got it. God says, "David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel…" (Jeremiah 33:17) Never lack means there will always be a man for it. That's a promise with no expiration date.

That's right. God says the priests who are Levites will always have a man before Him "…to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to present sacrifices." (Jeremiah 33:18) Those are the duties He names. Every time I read a list like that I think of my own busy mornings in the bakery.

Guard duty is an important job, but the verse doesn't list it. God says a man will be before Him "…to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to present sacrifices." (Jeremiah 33:18) The work He names is about offerings.

Reading aloud is a fine thing to do, friend, but it's not what this verse names. God says a man will be there "…to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to present sacrifices." (Jeremiah 33:18) The verse is about offerings.

Yes! God says, "If you can break My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night… then My covenant may also be broken with David My servant." (Jeremiah 33:20-21) And nobody can break the day and night. Every sunrise is a little reminder.

Rain and snow are a good guess, since they keep to their seasons too. But this verse names a different pair: "…My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night…" (Jeremiah 33:20) That's the one God puts next to His promise to David.
Mountains feel pretty unbreakable, I'll give you that. But God doesn't name them here. He says, "If you can break My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night…" (Jeremiah 33:20)

Not quite, friend. God says that only if the day and night could stop keeping their appointed times could His covenant with David and the Levites be broken. (Jeremiah 33:20-21) And day and night keep showing up. He's using the steady sunrise as the comparison.

That's right. God says His covenant with David could be broken only if His covenant with the day and the night could be broken, so that they stopped keeping their appointed time. (Jeremiah 33:20-21) Day and night aren't breaking. That's the whole comparison.

That's it. God says, "As the hosts of heaven cannot be counted and as the sand on the seashore cannot be measured, so too will I multiply the descendants of My servant David and the Levites who minister before Me." (Jeremiah 33:22) The hosts of heaven and the sand on the seashore are the two things He sets beside them. That's a lot of descendants.
Grass is a lot to count, I'll give you that. But the verse picks another comparison: "…the sand on the seashore cannot be measured…" (Jeremiah 33:22) That's what God sets next to the hosts of heaven.

Leaves are a good guess, friend, because trying to count them would take forever. But God doesn't use them here. He says, "As the hosts of heaven cannot be counted and as the sand on the seashore cannot be measured…" (Jeremiah 33:22)

Right. God says, "So they despise My people and no longer regard them as a nation." (Jeremiah 33:24) It comes from what these people are saying: that the LORD has rejected the two families He chose. I think that's a hurtful thing to say about anyone.

Honor would be a nicer ending, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. God says, "So they despise My people and no longer regard them as a nation." (Jeremiah 33:24) Honor is the opposite of despise. These people are saying the LORD has rejected the two families He chose.

Fear is a strong word, but it's not the one here. God says, "So they despise My people and no longer regard them as a nation." (Jeremiah 33:24) To despise is to look down on someone, while to fear is to be afraid of them. The verse says despise, and nothing about being afraid.
Yes, friend. God closes with this: "For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them." (Jeremiah 33:26) That's how the passage ends. It's a gentle ending, and I like it.

It's an easy word to reach for after a heavy chapter, but it's not the one God uses. He says, "For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them." (Jeremiah 33:26) The last word is compassion.

Judgment shows up earlier in the passage, so I can see why that came to mind. But God ends with something else: "For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them." (Jeremiah 33:26) He finishes on compassion, friend.
